source.notes: Found on the official page https://cisce.org/specimen-question-papers-isc-class-xii-2027/. This is a SPECIMEN paper for the 2027 ISC examination (examYear=2027), not a past board exam. The single PDF contains both the question paper (11 printed pages, PDF pages 1-11) and an 'ANSWER KEY' (7 printed pages, PDF pages 12-19); answerSourceUrl is the same URL, answerSourceFile is null. Printed instructions: 'Maximum Marks: 70', 'Time Allotted: Three Hours', plus an additional fifteen minutes' reading time (not included in durationMinutes). Twenty questions in four sections: Section A (Question 1, fourteen one-mark subparts, 14 marks), Section B (Questions 2-8, seven two-mark questions, 14 marks), Section C (Questions 9-17, nine three-mark questions, 27 marks), Section D (Questions 18-20, three five-mark questions, 15 marks). 'Internal choices have been provided in two questions each in Sections B, C and D' (Q2/Q4 in B, Q9/Q10 in C, Q18/Q19 in D); these OR pairs are split into two entries sharing a choiceGroup, each carrying the full question marks (not divided), per the brief. Question 1 is printed as (A) seven MCQ subparts (i)-(vii) then (B) seven short-answer subparts (i)-(vii), each with its own printed [1] mark; to keep (number, part) unique this pack labels them '(A)(i)'..'(A)(vii)' and '(B)(i)'..'(B)(vii)' (the nesting as printed, concatenated). Every other multi-part question in Sections B/C/D (i.e. one that is NOT one half of an OR pair) prints only a single total mark value for the whole question, with no marks given for its individual (i)/(ii)/(iii)/(a)/(b) sub-parts; per the brief's rule those sub-parts are kept together as one entry (type CASE_BASED, SHORT_ANSWER or LONG_ANSWER depending on whether a shared stem/scenario/figure ties the sub-parts together) using the printed total marks. This paper prints a cognitive-level tag next to nearly every item/sub-part, using the words (Recall), (Understand), (Apply), (Analyse), (Evaluate); recorded verbatim without the parentheses as cognitiveLevel. Where a merged multi-part entry's sub-parts carry different tags, cognitiveLevel is omitted on that entry and the per-sub-part tags are listed in extractionIssues instead (the tags are kept out of the text field itself); where all sub-parts of a merged entry share the same tag, that single tag is used. The marking-scheme (answer key) formulas are frequently badly broken across lines/columns by the PDF text extraction, worst in Q8, Q9(i)/(ii), Q10(i)/(ii), Q14, Q18(i)/(ii), Q19(i)/(ii) and Q20: for these, officialAnswer keeps only the printed final results/values and any surrounding words that extracted cleanly; the multi-step equation working itself is NOT reconstructed from standard physics formulas and is dropped, each flagged 'Official answer partly missing in extraction (equation working not in the text layer); see page N' and set to LOW confidence. A small number of one-line, single split fraction/power fixes elsewhere (e.g. Q2(i)/(ii), Q4(ii), and the final result lines in Q10, Q19(i)(b)) were reflowed inline since they are unambiguous and confined to one formula, flagged 'Notation rebuilt from the PDF layout (fractions/powers); check against the PDF' with MEDIUM confidence where nothing else is wrong with that entry. Simple same-line flattened sub/superscripts (e.g. '10-17C', 'x2', 'A1/3', 'mu1') are kept exactly as printed and flagged 'Superscript/subscript flattened: ...' without necessarily lowering confidence. Q1(A)(iv)'s printed two-column match table and Q14's two-row prism table are reflowed into plain sentences preserving every value (no data lost, so hasFigure is false for those). Several questions depend on a diagram or graph that is not reproducible as text and could not be answered without it, so are set to LOW confidence with a hasFigure issue: Q1(A)(i) and Q1(A)(iii) (Figures 1/2, relative positions of points/wire), Q10(i) (Figure 4 - only 4 of the paper's own 'five other resistors' are visible in the extracted text; the fifth, R5 = 40 ohm, is recoverable only from the official answer), Q10(ii) (Figure 5, Wheatstone-bridge/meter-bridge layout), Q11 (Figure 6, direction of v relative to B), Q12 (Figure 7, needed only for sub-part (ii)), Q16 (Figure 9, three photoelectric images, only image B's photon energy is given as text), and Q18(i) (a current-vs-time graph; the period and peak current used in the official answer are read off the graph, not stated as text). Q3's official answer is itself an unreproduced circuit diagram (the extracted text shows only point labels 'P' and 'Q'); Q18(ii)(a)'s official answer is likewise a drawn one-cycle sine graph not reproduced as text; both are flagged with 'Official answer partly missing in extraction (figure/equation)'. accessedOn 2026-09-28.

questions.text: How can the focal length of a given convex lens be measured in Physics laboratory using only a metre scale?

officialAnswer.text: The focal length of a convex lens can be measured using only a metre scale through the Distant Object Method. This method relies on focusing light rays from a very distant source onto a surface to find the lens's focal point.

questions.text: What is the difference between a moving metallic ball colliding with another ball in motion and a photon colliding with an electron?

officialAnswer.text: When a photon collides with an electron, it loses either its entire energy or none at all, whereas a moving ball can lose any fraction of its energy.

officialAnswer.text: The gamma ray photon should have the minimum energy of 2(mp)c2. Or The gamma ray photon should have the Combined Minimum Energy E = 938·3 + 938·3 = 1876·6MeV.

questions.text: Explain why resistance of a semiconductor material decreases when its temperature is increased.

officialAnswer.text: As temperature rises, large number of electrons break their covalent bonds and cross the forbidden band gap into the conduction band. Thus, there are large number of free electrons in the conduction band which result in reduction in resistance.

questions.text:
(i) Why the current flowing is extremely small during reverse biasing of a junction diode?
(ii) Extrinsic semiconductors are neither good nor bad conductors of electricity. Why are they still considered useful?
extractionIssues: Marks for Question 7 are printed only as a single total [2] for the whole question, not per sub-part (i)/(ii); kept as one entry per the brief.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) The current flowing through the diode during reverse bias is extremely small because it is entirely due to minority charge carriers, which are much smaller in number (in comparison with number of majority carriers).
(ii) Extrinsic semiconductors are highly useful because their electrical conductivity can be precisely controlled, tuned, and manipulated by altering the concentration of dopant atoms (impurities) added to the crystal.
Or
Electronic devices like diodes, transistors, solar cells etc. can be made out of extrinsic semiconductors, which have many applications in electronic gadgets.

questions.text:
An alpha particle is moving with a velocity v. It enters a uniform magnetic field (B) as shown below. The magnetic field is perpendicular and into the plane of the paper. A uniform electric field is applied in the same region as the magnetic field so that the alpha particle passes undeviated through the combined fields.
(i) What should be the direction of the electric field?
(ii) Without any change in the electric and magnetic field, the alpha particle is replaced by a proton moving with a velocity v. Will there be any change in the path of the particle? Give a reason for your answer.
extractionIssues: Figure 6 (velocity-selector diagram showing the direction of v relative to B) on page 7 not reproduced; the exact geometry needed to answer part (i) is not in the extracted text.
Vector-arrow glyphs over E and B did not extract cleanly (rendered as stray characters in the marking scheme); reconstructed as plain E, B.
Cognitive-level tags printed per sub-part: (i) Analyse, (ii) Evaluate — not captured in a single cognitiveLevel field because they differ per sub-part.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) The electric field should be in the plane of the paper, pointing vertically downwards.
(ii) Since the alpha particle travels undeviated, the magnetic force equals the electric force: Bqv = qE, so v = E/B. Since protons also obey the same relation (same v, same E and same B), they will also travel undeviated.

questions.text:

(iii) Why is steel preferred to soft iron in making permanent magnets.

(i) Magnetic field inside a solenoid is uniform whereas magnetic field along the axis of a circular coil is non-uniform.
(ii) In anticlockwise direction (according to Lenz's law).
(iii) It has a large coercive force i.e. it is more difficult to demagnetise steel than iron.

questions.text:
A physics teacher drew a ray diagram on the board as shown below and asked the following questions to the students. State whether the answer of the student is correct or incorrect. Correct the incorrect response with an explanation in brief.
(i) Teacher: There is a point P on the screen where the path difference between two interfering light waves is exactly 1·2 × 10-6 m. If the light emitted by the source has a wavelength of 600 nm, can anyone tell me whether a bright or a dark fringe will form at the point P?
Student: Dark fringe will be obtained.
(ii) Teacher: Two students performed the same Young's double slit experiment. One student obtained wider fringes. What is the possible reason for this observation?
Student: The student who obtained wider fringes must have increased the distance between the two slits.
(iii) Teacher: If one of the slits is closed with a finger while performing the experiment, what change will be noticed on the screen?
Student: The screen will get illuminated uniformly.
extractionIssues: Figure 8 (ray diagram) on page 8 not reproduced (illustrative; the numeric values needed for part (i) are given in the text).
Superscript flattened: 10-6

officialAnswer.text:
(i) Incorrect, bright fringe (since path difference = 2λ)
(ii) Incorrect, because the slit separation should have been decreased.
(iii) Incorrect, diffraction pattern is seen on the screen.

questions.text:

questions.text:
Study the images shown in Figure 9 below given below carefully and answer the questions that follow. (All three surfaces have same work function = 2·3eV)
(i) Why are no photoelectrons emitted in image 'A'?
(ii) Which image corresponds to the highest stopping potential?
(iii) If the photon energy in image B = 2·8 eV, calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photo electrons.
extractionIssues: Figure 9 (three images A, B, C showing incident photon energies/currents for a photoelectric-effect setup) on page 9 not reproduced; parts (i) and (ii) cannot be answered from the extracted text alone (only image B's photon energy, 2·8 eV, is given in text).
Cognitive-level tags printed per sub-part: (i) Analyse, (ii) Recall, (iii) Apply — not captured in a single cognitiveLevel field because they differ per sub-part.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) No photoelectrons are emitted because the energy of the incident photons is less than the work function of the material. For photoelectric emission to take place, the incident photon energy must be greater than or equal to the threshold work function.
(ii) C
(iii) Using Einstein's photoelectric equation: Kmax = E − φ = 2·8 − 2·3 = 0·5eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons in image B is 0·5 eV.

questions.text:
(i) What is a solar cell?
(ii) Explain its working in brief.
(iii) In an energy band diagram of a certain material, forbidden band is absent. Identify the material.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) A solar cell (also known as a photovoltaic cell) is a semiconductor p-n junction diode that directly converts solar energy (light energy) into electrical energy.
(ii) The incoming photons break covalent bonds near the junction, generating free electron-hole pairs. This build-up of charges creates a voltage difference (electromotive force). When an external load or circuit is connected, a direct electric current begins to flow.
(iii) Metal

questions.text:
(a) Assuming that nuclei are spherical in shape, whose radius R is given by R = R0A1/3 where R0 is a constant, show that the nuclear density (i.e. density of nuclear matter) is independent of mass number (A) of the nucleus / atom.

questions.text:
An innovative optical sensor system for a miniature drone incorporates a combination of various optical elements. A beam of light from an LED source first passes through a convex spherical refracting surface (radius of curvature R = 20 cm) separating air μ1= 1·0 from a glass medium of refractive index μ2= 1·5. The light then enters a thin biconvex lens of focal length 10 cm. Finally, the beam strikes a concave spherical mirror of radius of curvature 30 cm, which acts as a collector, focusing the rays onto a photodetector (optical instrument application) to measure light intensity.
(i) If the drone operates in a highly humid or misty environment where a film of water completely coats the lens surfaces, how will the refractive power of this lens change?
(ii) A point object is placed in air at a distance of 60 cm in front of the convex spherical refracting surface. What is the position of the image formed by this surface?
(iii) If this setup is to be modified to function as a reflecting astronomical telescope, what roles would be played by the mirror and the lens?
(iv) Which mirror collects light from a distant object most efficiently?
extractionIssues: Subscript flattened: μ1, μ2
Cognitive-level tags printed per sub-part: (i) Apply, (ii) Understand, (iii) Understand, (iv) Recall — not captured in a single cognitiveLevel field because they differ per sub-part.
Official answer partly missing in extraction (equation working not in the text layer for part (ii)); see page 19

officialAnswer.text:
